For a year Nazia had blamed 'those tech-park people' for everything in Bengaluru: the rents, the traffic, her landlord's new rules. Online she called them locusts.
Then, on a wet Tuesday evening, her scooter died on the Outer Ring Road. Cars sprayed past. A young woman in a company lanyard pulled over, held an umbrella over the engine while Nazia tried the kick-start, then called a mechanic she knew and waited forty minutes with her.
Her name was Bidisha. She'd moved from Siliguri two years ago. She shared a flat with three others because the rent was too high for her, too.
'Rent's too high for you as well?' Nazia said, surprised.
'Everyone I know is struggling,' Bidisha said. 'Where are you from?'
On the way home, Nazia didn't open the forums. She found herself wondering about Bidisha's flat, her three flatmates, her family in Siliguri. She had a question she wanted to ask her.

'Jeevan-da, you seen this? Those colony people again. Every one of them.'
'Show me.' Jeevan put down his tea and actually watched the video. 'Hm. Who made it?'
'Does it matter? It's true.'
'Maybe. I'm just curious.' Jeevan scratched his beard. 'You've been angry at them for a year, Anirban. Have you met one?'
'Why would I?'
'I'm asking honestly. Name one.'
A pause. 'There's a guy at the gym. Sanjay. He's from there.'
'What's he like?'
Another pause. 'He spots me on the bench press. Helped me with my back last month.'
'So Sanjay's okay.'
'Sanjay's different.'
'Maybe. How many of them have you met who weren't different?'
Anirban opened his mouth, then closed it.
'I'm not trying to win,' Jeevan said. 'I just want to know what you think. Not what the video thinks.'
Anirban looked at the paused screen for a while. 'I'll ask Sanjay where he grew up.'

Last winter I was sure I knew everything about "those people". I'd been reading about them every night for a year.
Then my scooter skidded on a wet road outside Pune, and I lay on the tarmac with my ankle twisted under me. The first person to stop was a young man named Darshan, from exactly the group I had spent a year mocking online. He held an umbrella over me, called my sister from my phone, and waited with me for forty minutes until she came. He talked about his daughter's school play so I wouldn't think about the pain.
He knew nothing about my posts. He just helped.
Afterwards I didn't have a big realisation. I had a question: what else don't I know about them? I started reading, meeting people, asking. Curiosity did what a hundred arguments hadn't. I'm Nikita, and I still have his umbrella.

qa.a: Forty minutes.

Supervisor's note, packing unit, Friday
Over recent months Raghav has made several remarks at lunch about "people like Ganga's lot", meaning the community Ganga comes from. I have spoken to him about it twice.
This week something shifted. Raghav's mother was admitted to hospital on Tuesday, and he was frantic about his shifts. Ganga quietly swapped three of her shifts with him without being asked and brought him food from home. On Thursday I saw Raghav at the gate asking her questions: where her family is from, what her village festival is like. He listened more than he talked.
Today he told me, "I didn't know she has a son in college. I didn't know anything, really." He asked to be paired with her on the new line.

Tuesday
Bidisha came over tonight. She's the only one in the family still talking to me after the Diwali fight. I started ranting again, the usual, about how that whole group is ruining everything. I expected her to argue like everyone does, and I was ready.
She didn't argue. She asked, "Have you ever actually spoken to one of them? Properly?"
I said I didn't need to. She said, "Just curious. What do you imagine they're like at home?"
I couldn't answer. I realised I only had pictures from videos. No faces.
Then she told me about her flatmate from that community, who sat up with her all night when she had dengue last year. She said it plainly, not to win anything.
I didn't change my mind tonight. But I keep thinking of her flatmate holding a bucket at 3 a.m. That's a person. I don't know what to do with that yet.
Kiran
